title: Effects of architectural interventions on psychological, cognitive, social, and pro-environmental aspects of occupant well-being: Results from an immersive online study
research_question: To evaluate the influence of built features (materials, windows, and diversity cues) on four well-being outcomes: sense of belonging, stress, creativity, and pro-environmental concern, using an immersive online survey.

participants.description: Participants were located in the United States and were over 18 years of age. Mean age was 37.5 years (SD 12.3), median 34.0 [18.0, 71.0]. Gender: 60.6% Man, 38.4% Woman, 0.5% Non Binary, 0.5% Prefer Not to Say. Race: 70.8% White, 8.5% Asian, 7.8% Black or African American, 5.1% Latinx, 6.8% Multiple, 1.0% Prefer not to say. Education: 55.5% Bachelor's or higher, 44.0% Less than a Bachelor's, 0.5% Prefer not to say.
participants.recruitment: Recruited through Prolific, an online crowdsourcing platform.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Participants were shown multiple pictures and a 40-second panoramic video of an indoor office space. The space was manipulated across eight (2x2x2) factorial conditions: 1) Materials (natural: wooden table, chairs, frames vs. artificial: metal table, chairs, frames), 2) Windows (presence vs. absence), and 3) Representation (photographic decor with diverse people vs. non-diverse people).

measures.instrument: Revised version of the Sense of Social and Academic Fit scale (6 items)
Valence (7-point Likert) and Arousal (7-point Likert) items
Positive and Negative Affect Schedules (PANAS) scale
Condensed version of the Connectedness to Nature Scale
Percentage of $50 raffle winnings donated to a tree-planting organization

the presence of windows lead to significantly higher positive affect scores (p = 0.007**) compared to the absence of windows
gender appears as a significant predictor of positive affect (F (395) = 4.04, p = 0.045*, ges = 0.01), with scores being lower for women

mechanisms: Diverse representation signaled an inclusive environment, leading to participants feeling psychologically safe and subsequently creating conditions conducive to creative thinking.
The connection to nature through urban green spaces and biophilia theory suggests indoor natural elements may play a role in building occupant sense of belonging.
implementation_implications: Immersive online surveys are an effective and efficient approach for built environment research, reducing costs, time, and resources while increasing participant diversity.

The presence of windows, natural materials, and diverse photographic decor can be used to promote sense of belonging, reduce negative affect, increase positive affect, and enhance divergent and self-reported creativity.

tables.description: Demographic information of the after-exclusions sample, including gender, age, race, and education level.
Mean and standard deviation of all measured dependent variables across each level of the independent variables (Natural/Artificial materials, Windows/No Windows, Diverse/Non-Diverse Representation).

ANOVA results with outliers included, showing F-statistics, p-values, and partial eta-squared for main effects of Materials, Windows, Representation, and their interactions on all dependent variables.
key_stats: Negative Affect: F=6.37, p=0.012, partial n²=0.016 (Materials)
Positive Affect: F=7.44, p=0.007, partial n²=0.018 (Windows)
Divergent Creativity: F=18.6, p<0.001, partial n²=0.044 (Representation)

limitations: Inability to control the actual built environment where participants took the survey (e.g., presence of natural light, ambient sounds, other people).
Online studies are not well-suited for testing tactile and olfactory aspects of the built environment.
Photographs/videos of windows cannot fully reproduce the biological benefits or negative effects (e.g., glare, thermal discomfort) of true natural light.
Small effect sizes for significant results, possibly due to limited exposure duration (<1 hour) to built features.
The study used only two levels for each independent variable (e.g., presence/absence), limiting investigation into the quantity of elements (e.g., number/size of windows).
